entry.title: One Click Can Change Your Life
entry.description: I’ve been thinking about this idea for a while.
entry.body:
I’ve been thinking about this idea for a while.

Most of the decisions that shape your life do not feel important when you make them. They usually look like small choices made without much thought: clicking on a video, opening a link, trying a tool, talking to someone, going to an event, starting a project, or picking up a book.

Recently, my English teacher took our class to the school library and had us choose a book. I picked *Fluke: Chance, Chaos, and Why Everything We Do Matters* by Brian Klaas.

I have not read it yet, so I am not going to summarize or analyze it. But the premise reminded me of this idea and made me want to write about it again. I may write a separate blog about the book after I finish it.

![Screenshot 2026-08-22](https://cdn.egeuysal.com/content/2026/08/22/asset-01.png)

## The first click is usually unremarkable

At some point, I clicked on a YouTube video featuring Tanay Kothari, the founder of Wispr Flow.

I do not remember treating the click like an important decision. I probably expected to watch an interesting video and spend a few minutes thinking about it. Instead, I came away with new ways of thinking about software, products, and workflows.

The video gave me questions I would not have asked before. It made me pay more attention to how software fits into someone’s actual life, not just whether the product technically works. It changed the way I looked at some of the problems I was already interested in.

Nothing about the click itself felt significant.

The same thing happens with random links people post on X. Sometimes I open one, try a tool for a few minutes, and never use it again. Other times, the tool becomes a permanent part of my workflow.

A small decision can introduce a new way to write, build, research, communicate, or organize my day. Sometimes it changes only one part of my workflow. Sometimes that one part changes what I do next.

I could have scrolled past.

If I had, my workflow might have developed differently. I would not know what I missed because I would never have seen the alternative.

That is what makes these decisions difficult to understand. You cannot compare the life you lived with the life that would have happened if you had clicked.

## My life is mostly a chain of small decisions

When I look at my own life, it is difficult to find one moment that explains everything.

I started coding when I was young. I shipped my first SaaS product at fifteen. Now I spend a lot of my time balancing school with building products like Ryva.

Those things sound more intentional when I describe them afterward than they felt while they were happening.

I did not wake up one morning with a complete plan to become a founder. I clicked through tutorials. I opened documentation because I did not understand something. I tried to fix bugs that seemed impossible. I found projects online and wondered how they worked. I watched people explain products and wondered why they had made certain decisions.

One choice led to another choice.

A tutorial led to a small project. The project led to a problem. The problem led to a search. The search led to a tool, a person, or an idea. Eventually, those small actions became enough experience to build something real.

The same thing is happening with Ryva. Building a product is not one big decision. It is a long collection of smaller ones: deciding to investigate a problem, deciding to talk to someone, deciding to rebuild a feature, deciding to keep working after a quiet launch, and deciding to look at the problem from another angle.

Some of those decisions will matter. Most will not.

I do not think any single click explains my life. That would make the story too simple. But I do think the direction of my life has been shaped by staying open to enough small possibilities.

Moving from Turkey to the United States also made this more obvious to me. The internet allowed me to learn about software, English, startups, and people who lived far away from me before I ever met most of them. Geography still matters, but the internet can create paths that would not exist otherwise.

A random video can connect you to a new idea. A documentation page can help you build something. A conversation with someone online can change what you think is possible.

A click can quietly make the world larger.

## We judge opportunities by their immediate cost

I think people often evaluate opportunities too narrowly.

We ask whether something is worth the next twenty minutes, the next hour, or the effort required right now. That is useful when we are protecting our time, but it becomes limiting when immediate payoff is the only thing we consider.

| Immediate thought | What it ignores |
| --- | --- |
| This video will waste 20 minutes. | It might give me an idea I use for years. |
| This tool probably will not be useful. | It might change how I work every day. |
| This event might be boring. | I might meet someone who changes my direction. |
| This project might fail. | I might learn the skill needed for the next project. |
| This conversation might lead nowhere. | It might change how I understand the problem. |

The problem is not that these thoughts are always wrong.

The video might waste twenty minutes. The tool might be useless. The event might be boring. The project might fail. The conversation might lead nowhere.

The problem is that we often treat the immediate cost as certain and the possible benefit as irrelevant.

We know exactly what twenty minutes costs. We do not know what it could lead to. Because the future consequence is uncertain, we often treat it as if it does not exist.

But many important outcomes begin with an uncertain action.

A project can lead to a skill. A skill can lead to a product. A product can lead to a customer. A customer can lead to a new understanding of a market. That understanding can lead to a completely different company.

The first action does not need to contain the final result. It only needs to create the possibility of the next action.

## Turning points are easier to see backward

The strange thing about important moments is that they rarely announce themselves.

When you are inside the moment, you are usually thinking about something much smaller. You are deciding whether to watch a video, send a message, attend an event, or spend an hour learning something new.

You are not thinking, “This may become part of the story I tell about my life.”

There is no label that says a decision will matter later.

Looking backward makes everything appear more connected. You can trace a project to a conversation, a habit to a video, a friendship to an event, or a new direction to a random link.

But looking forward is different. From the present, you cannot see the whole chain.

![Screenshot 2026-08-22](https://cdn.egeuysal.com/content/2026/08/22/asset-02.png)

That is why it is so difficult to know which opportunities deserve attention. You are making decisions without knowing their consequences.

You have to make the best judgment you can with the information available. But you also have to accept that some valuable things will only become valuable after you try them.

## This does not mean saying yes to everything

I am not arguing that people should accept every opportunity.

Time matters. Attention matters. There are too many links, tools, events, and ideas to explore all of them. Constantly chasing new things can become another form of procrastination.

Some opportunities have a high downside. Some are obviously distractions. Some projects should be abandoned. Some conversations should not be continued.

The point is not to remove all filtering. The point is to avoid filtering too aggressively when the downside is small.

A useful filter might be:

1. Does this genuinely interest me?
2. Is the downside manageable?
3. Can I try it without making a major commitment?
4. Could it introduce a useful idea, person, skill, or direction?
5. Will I regret ignoring it more than I would regret trying it?

If something passes that filter, it is probably worth giving it a real chance.

> If something genuinely interests you and the downside is small, give it a shot.

Click the link. Watch the video. Try the tool. Go to the event. Talk to the person. Start the project. Read the book.

You do not have to promise yourself that the opportunity will become important. You do not have to force it into a larger story. You only need to give yourself enough room to discover what happens next.

## Staying open without losing direction

There is a balance between curiosity and focus.

You cannot spend your entire life following every interesting possibility. Building anything meaningful requires staying with one problem long enough to understand it. School requires attention. Relationships require presence. Projects require repetition.

But focus should not mean becoming completely closed.

The best work often comes from combining a clear direction with enough openness to notice useful ideas. I can keep working on Ryva while still watching a video about a different product. I can care about a specific project while remaining curious about tools, people, and ideas outside it.

Sometimes the thing that seems unrelated gives me a better way to solve the problem I am already working on.

Most attempts will not change your life. That is normal.

The goal is not to turn every click into a life lesson. The goal is to avoid rejecting every possibility just because its value is not immediately visible.

You never know which seemingly insignificant decision will matter later.

Sometimes avoiding a small waste of time is less important than giving yourself the chance to discover something valuable.

The click feels small while you are making it. Only much later might you realize that it changed what you built, who you met, or where you decided to go next.
